caseStudy.water-access-kampala.title: When access to water becomes uncertain
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.summary: Listening to what communities are reporting about water access in Kampala
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.imageAlt: A crowded market street at sunset
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.1: Across communities in Kampala, access to water can change from one day to the next. Interruptions, unreliable supply and concerns about water quality can affect households differently depending on where they live and the services available to them.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.2: Through Community Water Watch, WatchTower provides a way for people to report these experiences in the languages they are most comfortable using, helping individual accounts become part of a broader picture of what communities are experiencing.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.3: We sometimes go days without knowing when the water will return.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.4: One report captures one person's experience. But when similar reports begin appearing across different places and at different times, they can reveal something more.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.5: Community Water Watch was created to bring these experiences together and make them easier to understand.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.6: Hearing what the numbers can miss
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.7: Traditional data can tell us a great deal about infrastructure and service delivery. But it may not always capture what unreliable access feels like at household and community level.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.8: People describe the days without water, the distances travelled to find alternatives, changes in water quality and the ways interruptions affect everyday life.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.9: Community reporting creates another layer of evidence, one grounded in what people are seeing and experiencing themselves.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.10.a: A crowded market street at sunset
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.12: Community Water Watch used WatchTower to make reporting accessible across languages and locations.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.14: People could submit reports in the languages they were most comfortable using, reducing the need for communities to translate their experiences before sharing them.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.16: Reports could be shared through text or voice, giving people different ways to describe what was happening.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.18: WatchTower helped transcribe, translate and organise reports so that information submitted in different languages could be understood together.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.20: Reports could then be explored across location, time and incident type, helping recurring reporting patterns become easier to identify.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.22: Personal information and precise locations can be limited or generalised where necessary to help protect people submitting reports.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.24: As reports accumulated, individual experiences started to connect.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.27: Reports were submitted from communities across Kampala, with concentrations of reporting around water availability, service interruptions and water quality.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.30: Listening is only useful if what communities share can inform what happens next.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.31: The evidence generated through Community Water Watch can support conversations between communities, organisations and other stakeholders working on water access.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.32: Reports can provide additional context for investigation, advocacy, planning, coordination and accountability.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.34: The people closest to an incident often understand dimensions of it that aggregate numbers alone cannot show.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.35: Community reporting provides a way to capture those experiences as they happen.
caseStudy.water-access-kampala.body.36: When people can report in their own languages and those reports can be understood, connected and explored together, individual voices can contribute to a clearer understanding of what is happening on the ground.
